message.content:
I don’t have a way to probe your connection from here, so I can’t tell you the exact speed right now.  
But you can check it yourself in a few quick ways:

---

## 1. Use an online speed‑test website  
The simplest method is to visit a site that runs a test in your browser.

| Site | How to use |
|------|------------|
| **Speedtest by Ookla** – <https://www.speedtest.net> | Click “Go” and wait for the test to finish. |
| **Fast.com** – <https://fast.com> | The test starts automatically; click “Show more info” for download/upload details. |
| **Google Speed Test** – type “speed test” into Google and click the built‑in test. | Click “Run Speed Test” and wait for results. |

These sites give you download speed, upload speed, and ping (latency).

---

## 2. Run a speed test from the command line (if you have Python)

If you prefer a terminal/command‑prompt approach, you can use the free `speedtest-cli` tool.

### a. Install `speedtest-cli`

```bash
# On Windows (PowerShell)
pip install speedtest-cli

# On macOS/Linux
sudo apt-get install speedtest-cli   # Debian/Ubuntu
brew install speedtest-cli           # macOS with Homebrew
```

### b. Run the test

```bash
speedtest
```

It will output something like:

```
Testing from Your ISP (Your City)...
Retrieving speedtest.net configuration...
Testing download speed........................................
Download:  85.23 Mbit/s
Testing upload speed..........................................
Upload:    12.45 Mbit/s
Ping:      24.7 ms
```

---

## 3. Use Windows built‑in “Network Speed Test”

If you’re on Windows 10/11:

1. Open **Settings** → **Network & Internet** → **Status**.
2. Click **Network speed test** (this opens a Microsoft Store app that runs a quick test).

---

## 4. Quick test via PowerShell (no extra installs)

If you just want a rough idea of download speed, you can use PowerShell to download a file and time it:

```powershell
$uri = "https://speed.hetzner.de/100MB.bin"   # 100 MB test file
$dest = "$env:TEMP\test.bin"
$sw = [System.Diagnostics.Stopwatch]::StartNew()
Invoke-WebRequest -Uri $uri -OutFile $dest
$sw.Stop()
$bytes = (Get-Item $dest).Length
$seconds = $sw.Elapsed.TotalSeconds
$mbps = ($bytes / 1MB) / $seconds
Write-Host "Download speed: $([math]::Round($mbps,2)) MB/s"
Remove-Item $dest
```

This script downloads a 100 MB file from Hetzner’s public test server and reports the average speed in MB/s.

---

### What to look for

| Metric | Typical values (for a good broadband connection) |
|--------|--------------------------------------------------|
| **Download** | 25 Mbps – 100 Mbps (or higher for fiber) |
| **Upload** | 5 Mbps – 20 Mbps |
| **Ping** | < 50 ms (lower is better) |

If your numbers are far below what your ISP advertises, you might want to:

1. Restart your modem/router.
2. Check for firmware updates.
3. Run tests at different times of day to see if congestion is an issue.
4. Contact your ISP if the problem persists.

Let me know if you’d like help interpreting the results or troubleshooting specific issues!
